---
title: "Capstone: Final Group Presentation"
---

The final for this class is a **group presentation (under 10 minutes)** exploring
a plant genetics topic of your group's choice, presented in class on
**December 1 and 3**. Groups are 4–5 people. It's worth 30% of your grade
(100 points, plus up to 5 extra credit).

## Start thinking about it now

The capstone comes at the end, but the best presentations start much
earlier — in two ways.

**The topic.** Ideas will come at you all quarter: a lecture that hooks you,
a reading, the cacao tour, a guest speaker, something you dig up researching
your midterm. When something makes you think "I want to know more about
that," write it down — that list is where good capstone topics come from.
Like the midterm, focused beats broad, and the same three doors apply: a
problem plant genetics can help solve, an open question, or how a genetic
technology works.

**The group.** This is a group project, which makes the class itself part of
the assignment: sit next to someone new, talk during the break, compare
answers during in-class activities. The people you meet in the first weeks
may well become your group — and groups that form around a shared interest
tend to have more fun with this. If you'd rather be assigned to a group,
that's completely fine too; the preference survey (due **Thu Oct 29**) asks
which you want.

## What you submit

- **Presentation file** (PDF or PPTX) — one upload per group on Canvas;
  anyone in the group can submit and it counts for everyone. Due Dec 1 at
  3:10 PM regardless of which day your group presents.
- **Individual contributions statement** — every student submits their own
  short, confidential statement: what you contributed (slides, research,
  figures, organizing, presenting sections…) and how the work was divided.
  A few sentences is plenty. Only the teaching team sees it; it's how we
  make sure credit lands where the work happened.

## What we're looking for

Think of your presentation as a short lecture to the rest of the class.
Your audience has taken the same course you have, so you can assume they
know what an allele, a QTL, or CRISPR is. What they don't know is your
topic. By the end of your talk, they should understand one plant
genetics story well: what the problem or question is, what is known about
the genetics behind it, how researchers figured that out, and what is
still unresolved.

**Go into the genetics.** A presentation that stays at the surface
("drought is a big problem for wheat, and genetics can help") will not score
well on depth. Strong presentations name the genes, alleles,
mutations, or loci involved, explain how they work (the mechanism), and
show the evidence: the experiment, the mapping study, the field trial, the
figure from the paper. If you can say "researchers found X, and we know
this because they did Y," you are at the right depth.

**But pitch it to your audience.** Going deep does not mean burying the
class in every detail from the paper. Pick the few genes, results, and
figures that tell the story, and explain them at a level your classmates
can follow. If the room is lost, the depth doesn't count for much.

**A shape that works:**

- **Introduction.** The background your audience needs and why the topic
  matters (a crop, a disease, a farmer's problem, a food security issue).
  Keep it short, but don't skip it.
- **Body.** The main portion. What is known about the genetics, how it was
  discovered, and how it is being used or could be used (breeding, gene
  editing, conservation, and so on). Give each slide one take-home message.
- **Conclusion.** Pull the key insights together and end on one clear
  message you want people to remember. Open questions and where the field
  is heading make a good ending.

**Slides.** Use figures, diagrams, and photos instead of walls of text, and
make sure every image is high enough resolution to read from the back of
the room. Put your citations on the slides where the claims are made, so
the audience can see where each fact comes from (at least 5 citations
total, in a consistent format, for papers and websites alike). A references
slide at the end is a good idea too.

**Time.** Under 10 minutes for the whole group, and aim for about 8. Practice
out loud together with a timer, more than once, and cut until you are under
10. Running long cuts into other groups' time, and a very short talk rarely
leaves room to explore the topic in depth.

**Working as a group.** We grade collaboration from how evenly the work was
shared, so build your slides in a shared file (for example Google Slides)
where the edit history shows who did what. Your individual statement should
match what the group did.

**Being in the audience.** Come both days and pay attention to the other
groups. Your group also has an assigned group to ask a question
([see the table above](#questions)), and good questions are part of what
makes these two days fun.

**Extra credit (up to 5 points)** goes to groups that bring something
genuinely their own: an original framing, a creative way of explaining the
genetics, a comparison or synthesis you won't find in a standard review.

## How it's graded {#rubric}

**100 points total, plus up to 5 extra credit.** Everything is one grade for
the whole group except the two rows marked *each student*.

| Criterion | Pts | What we're looking for |
|---|---|---|
| Depth of content | 10 | Goes past the surface into the genes, mechanisms, and evidence, pitched at a depth your classmates can follow. Too shallow or too deep both lose points. |
| Accuracy and relevance | 10 | Facts are correct, current, and on topic. |
| Use of references | 10 | At least 5 citations, on the slides where the claims are made, in a consistent format. |
| Introduction | 5 | The background your audience needs and why the topic matters. |
| Body | 10 | A clear structure with one take-home message per slide. |
| Conclusion | 5 | Pulls the key points together and ends on one clear message. |
| Clarity and conciseness | 10 | Easy to follow. No walls of text. |
| Slide design | 10 | Figures and images over text, sharp enough to read from the back of the room. |
| Collaboration | 10 | Work shared evenly across the group. |
| Time management and communication | 5 | Under 10 minutes, good pacing, clear delivery. |
| Individual contribution (*each student*) | 10 | Your contributions statement shows a real share of the work and matches the group's account. |
| Audience engagement (*each student*) | 5 | Present and paying attention to the other groups on both days. |
| Extra credit: novelty | up to 5 | Something genuinely your own: an original framing, a creative explanation, or a synthesis you won't find in a standard review. |
